The '''drop rate''' is the frequency at which a [[monster]] is expected to yield a certain item when killed by players. When calculating a drop rate, divide the number of times you have gotten the certain item, by the total number of that monster that you have killed. For example: *[[Bones]] have a 100% drop rate from [[chicken]]s. *[[Feather]]s have approximately a 75% drop rate from chickens. ==Drop rate== All items have a chance of being dropped that is expressible as a fraction (ex. 1/5 or "1 in 5") —their '''drop rate'''. Drop rates such as "1 in 5" do not guarantee such a drop will be obtained after 5 kills. Instead, it can be thought that on average, a player would receive the drop once per 5 kills, with the chance to receive more or less. For any drop that isn't extremely common, drop rates can be thought of to show how many kills it would take for a 63.2% chance at receiving at least one of the item (as explained below). Drop rates are treated independently from one to the next; meaning no previous drops decrease or increase the drop rates for future kills. While a player killing such a creature 30 times and not obtaining such a drop is ''unlikely'', the players' chance of their next kill obtaining the drop remains the same. An exception to this is if there is a [[bad luck mitigation]] mechanic listed on certain monsters and events; this will increase the chance of receiving a drop after a dry streak. While somewhat counter-intuitive, probability itself cannot be simply multiplied per drop. For example if one were to calculate the chance of receiving a drop at least once after 100 kills as 10%, it would not become 20% after 200 kills. If it was additive, then the chance after 1100 kills would be 110%, which is impossible as probabilities are '''always''' equal to or between 0 and 1. ===Common Terms=== A common list of terms is provided below: * '''Average''' or '''Expectation''' is fairly intuitive, though not to be confused with the probability; if players seek a 1 in 5 drop and kill a monster 10 times, the average would be 2 drops, though a player could receive more or less. However the average doesn't refer to a specific outcome, for example, killing a monster with a 1 in 5 drop 3 times, would yield 0.6 of that drop on average, which is impossible as an outcome itself. * '''Probability''' or '''Chance''' refers to the likelihood of a specific outcome occurring. This can never be below zero or above one. * '''Independent/Dependent''' refers to two events influence each others outcome. Generally drops are treated independently. * '''Probability Distribution''' is a mathematical function that defines the probabilities of certain occurrences in specific circumstances, such as the commonly used {{wp|binomial distribution}}. === 50/50 Chance === Perhaps a helpful statistic in understanding drop rates is the number of kills required to yield a 50/50 chance of dropping at least one of the desired item. This can be found using the following formula: \frac{\log(0.5)}{\log\left(1 - \frac{n}{d} \right) \cdot r} where 0.5 represents the 50% probability, ''n'' is the rarity numerator, ''d'' is the rarity denominator, and ''r'' is the number of rolls per kc. The base of the logarithm is arbitrary, assuming it is the same on both sides of the fraction. So for example, since the [[Elysian sigil]] has a drop rate of 1/4,095, and killing the [[Corporeal Beast]] offers one roll per kill, the amount of kills needed to achieve a 50/50 chance at the sigil drop is \frac{\log(0.5)}{\log\left(1 - \frac{n}{d} \right) \cdot r} = \frac{-0.301...}{\log\left(1 - \frac{1}{4095} \right) \cdot 1} = \frac{-0.301...}{\log\left(\frac{4094}{4095} \right)} = \frac{-0.301...}{-0.00010607...} \approx 2838 So you would need to kill the Corporeal Beast 2,838 times before getting a coin flip's chance at the sigil drop; and you have the same probability of getting no sigil after 5,676 kills (2,838 × 2) as you do flipping a coin twice and getting heads both times. ==Calculating the odds of receiving items== {{See also|Calculator:Dry calc}} If the [[King Black Dragon]] is expected to drop a [[draconic visage]] once out of 5,000 kills, then the probability of getting a drop from one kill is as follows: : \begin{align} & 1-\left(1-\frac{1}{5000}\right)^{1} \\ = & \ 1-\left(\frac{4999}{5000}\right)^{1}\\ = & \ 1 - 0.9998 \\ = & \ 0.0002 \\ \end{align} That is 0.02%. To find the drop chance in 5,000 kills, the expression inside the parenthesis can be raised to the 5,000th power, which yields a meagre 63.2% chance of getting a draconic visage, i.e. 1-\left(\frac{4999}{5000}\right)^{5000} \approx 0.632. More generally, while not holding true for extremely common drops, the chance of obtaining at least one drop, of chance \frac{1}{n} once you have n kills trends towards 1-\frac{1}{e}\approx0.6321... or 63.212%. This estimation becomes accurate extremely quickly for even moderately rare drops. This value can be determined by determining following limit. \lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(1-\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)^{x}\right)}=1-\frac{1}{e}\approx0.6321... In another example, the probability of receiving at least one [[draconic visage]] in a task of 234 [[Skeletal Wyvern]]s can be received by changing the drop rate and kill count in the equation: : \begin{align} & 1 - (1 - 0.0001)^{234} \\ = & \ 1 - 0.9999^{234} \\ \approx & \ 1 - 0.976871 \\ \approx & \ 0.023129 \end{align} Therefore, there is approximately a 2.3% chance of receiving at least one draconic visage during this task. === Dry streaks and the odds of receiving a drop === It is crucial to understand that there is a difference between the odds of receiving ''a drop'' P(X>0) and receiving ''exactly one'' drop P(X=1). Hence the probabilities are not the same. The example above calculates the odds of receiving any amount of visages from 1 to 5000, i.e. the odds of not going empty-handed. The term \left(\frac{4999}{5000}\right)^{5000} \approx 0.368 seen in the expression above describes the probability of ''not'' receiving an item P(X=0)or more commonly spoken of as a dry streak of length 5000. ===Binomial model=== Given a known drop rate of \frac{1}{x}, the chance of receiving such an item k times in n kills can be calculated using {{wp|binomial distribution}}. All the examples above are special cases where the amount of drops, k=0 or k>0. For finding the probability of obtaining an item at least once, rather than a specified number of times, the binomial coefficient can be simplified into this equation: :1 - (1 - p)^x, where (1-p)^x is calculating the probability of ''not'' receiving the item, and that is used to calculate the inverse. The probability of receiving an item k times in n kills with a drop rate of \frac{1}{x} = p follows: : \binom n k p^k(1-p)^{n-k}, where \binom n k =\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} As this formula can be rather tedious to work by hand, many prefer using a [https://stattrek.com/online-calculator/binomial.aspx binomial probability calculator] where you enter p,nand k. ===Reaching a percentile=== Similarly, the number of King Black Dragons needed to kill to have a 90% probability of getting one when you kill them: : \begin{align} 1-\left(1-\frac{1}{5000}\right)^{x} &= 0.90 \\ x &= \frac{\log(1-0.9)}{\log(\frac{4999}{5000})} \\ x &= 11511.774\ldots \approx 11512 \end{align} This yields the answer 11,512 meaning that you need to kill 11,512 for at least 90% chance of getting a draconic visage. ===Back to back drops=== Again, using the [[King Black Dragon]] expected to drop a [[draconic visage]] once out of 5,000 kills, the probability of getting said drop twice from two kills or back-to-back is as follows: : \left(\frac{1}{5000}\right)^{2} =\ 0.00000004 = 0.000004\% For a back to back streak of any desired length, simply exchange the exponent. This is equivalent to using the binomial model and solving for the probability of receiving an item n times in nattempts. ==Expected Waiting Time== The Expected Waiting Time (notated E[T]) is the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value Expected Number] of kills/rolls/gambles to receive an item or collection of items from a drop table. The formulas to calculate the expected waiting time vary based on the specifics of the item(s) desired, their drop rate, and the drop table mechanics involved. ===Singular Item=== The expected waiting time to receive a singular item is the expected value of the geometric distribution with probability p.
E[T(p)] = \frac{1}{p}
Example: What is the expected number of kills of [[Corporeal Beast]] to receive at least one [[Elysian sigil]]?
p = \frac{1}{4095} E[T(p)] = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{4095}} = 4095
===Classical Coupon Collector's Problem=== The expected waiting time to receive at least one of each of n distinct items can be found in the mathematical literature under solutions to [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupon_collector%27s_problem the Coupon collector's problem]. The solution to the classical coupon collector's problem (CCCP) is:
E[T_n] = n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}
Example: How many pieces of the [[Evil chicken outfit]] on average should a player have received to expect to have receive at least one of all 4 pieces?
E[T_4] = 4\sum_{i=1}^{4}\frac{1}{i} = 4H_4{{efn|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i} will often be notated H_n where H_n is the nth [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_number Harmonic number]}} = \frac{25}{3} \approx [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=4H%284%29 8.3333]
===Multiple Items from Unequal Distributions=== The CCCP assumes at each instance the collector receives a coupon. ie. p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_n = 1 where p_i is the probability of receiving the ith item. It also assumes that p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_n. However, often the set of items of interest is often only a subset of the overall drop table. ie. p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_n < 1 and the probabilities of each item in the set are often not equal. The following two formulas solve for these issues ::*Let S_i = \left\{ J \subseteq \left\{1, \cdots , i\right\}\right\}. ie. All combinations of subsets of items of size i.
p_0 = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i. P_J = \sum_{j \in J}p_j. E[T_n(P)] = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{n-1-i}\sum_{J \in S_i} \frac{1}{1-(p_0+P_J)}{{CiteGeneral|url=https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.5245|title=New results on a generalized coupon collector problem using Markov chains|author=Emmanuelle Anceaume and Yann Busnel and Bruno Sericola|year=2014|work=arXiv}}
This formula grows rapidly with the size of the set of items of interest. After a modest number of items it becomes intractable even for powerful computers. However, for most drop sets of < ~10 items it is trivially solved. An alternate formula using [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution poissonization] can solve larger sets using numerical approximation methods.
E[T_n(P)] = \int_0^{\infty}\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-e^{-p_it}\right)\right)dt{{CiteGeneral|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2307466|title=Coupon collecting for unequal probabilities|accessdate=4 May 2023|author=H. von Schelling|year=1954|month=May|work=American Mathematical Monthly (Vol. 61, No. 5)|pages=306-311}}
Example: What is the expected number of kills of [[Corporeal Beast]] to receive at least one of each [https://oldschool.runescape.wiki/w/Corporeal_Beast#Sigils sigil], a [[Spirit shield]], and a [[Holy elixir]]?
n = 5 P = \left\{\frac{1}{4095}, \frac{1}{1365}, \frac{1}{1365}, \frac{8}{512}, \frac{3}{512}\right\} E[T_n(P)] = \int_0^{\infty}\left(1-\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{4095}}\right)\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{1365}}\right)^{2}\left(1-e^{-\frac{8t}{512}}\right)\left(1-e^{-\frac{3t}{512}}\right)\right)dt \approx [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=Integrate%5B1+-+%281+-+Exp%5B-t%2F4095%5D%29*%281+-+Exp%5B-t%2F1365%5D%29%5E2*%281+-+Exp%5B-8+t%2F512%5D%29*%281+-+Exp%5B-3+t%2F512%5D%29%2C+%7Bt%2C0%2CInfinity%7D%5D 4680.4]
===Multiple Copies of Items and Sets=== There are some bosses in the game which have drops which are always received in a sequential order without duplicates. For example [[Abyssal sire]] and [[Araxxor]] will drop the [[Abyssal bludgeon]] and [[Noxious halberd]] pieces in order. When modeling these expected waiting time for sets which include these items they can be thought of as a single item which must be receive a certain multiple of times. To calculate the expected waiting time of a set of items which are desired in different quantities the following formula can be applied. ::*Let K be the set of quotas desired for each item with k_i being the quota for the ith item. ::*Let T_n^{(K)}(P) be the random variable for the waiting time to complete k_i copies of the the ith item. ::*Let e_{k}(x) be 1 + x + \frac{x^{2}}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{x^{k}}{k!}, the kth order Taylor polynomial of the exponential function.
E[T_n^{(K)}(P)] = \int_{0}^{\infty} \left[1 - \prod_{i=1}^{m}\left(1 - e^{-p_i t} e_{k_i-1}(p_i t)\right)\right] dt{{CiteGeneral|url=https://web.cs.wpi.edu/~hofri/CCP.pdf|title=THE COUPON-COLLECTOR PROBLEM REVISITED|author=Boneh and Hofri|year=1997|work=Revised version of Stochastic Models, 13, #1 39−66|pages=10-11}}
Example: A team of 2 [[Group ironmen]] want to collect 2 sets of [[Bandos chestplate]], [[Bandos tassets]], [[Bandos hilt]]
P = \left\{\frac{1}{308}, \frac{1}{308}, \frac{1}{512}\right\} E[T_3^{(2)}(P)] = \int_{0}^{\infty} \left[1 - \left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{308}}\left(1+\frac{t}{308}\right)\right)^{2}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{512}}\left(1+\frac{t}{512}\right)\right)\right] dt \approx [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=integrate+1+-+%281+-+exp%28-t%2F308%29*%281+%2B+t%2F308%29%29%5E2*%281+-+exp%28-t%2F512%29*%281+%2B+t%2F512%29%29+from+t%3D0+to+infinity 1259.5]
Example: A player wants to collect the [[Araxite fang]] and Complete a [[Noxious halberd]].
P = \left\{\frac{1}{600}, \frac{1}{200}\right\} K = \left\{1, 3\right\} E[T_4^{(K)}(P)] = \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[1-\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{600}}\right)\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{200}}\left(1+\frac{t}{200}+\frac{t^2}{80000}\right)\right)\right]dt = [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%5Cint_%7B0%7D%5E%7B%5Cinfty%7D%5Cleft%5B1-%5Cleft%281-e%5E%7B-%5Cfrac%7Bt%7D%7B600%7D%7D%5Cright%29%5Cleft%281-e%5E%7B-%5Cfrac%7Bt%7D%7B200%7D%7D%5Cleft%281%2B%5Cfrac%7Bt%7D%7B200%7D%2B%5Cfrac%7Bt%5E2%7D%7B80000%7D%5Cright%29%5Cright%29%5Cright%5Ddt+ 853.125]
Another use case for this unequal quotas formula is when players are interested in completing a particular section of the [[Collection log]] while also obtaining a certain number of duplicates of specific items for other uses. For example an Ironman wants to complete the [[Glough's experiments]] section of the Collection log while also obtaining 4 total [[Zenite shard]]. ===Multiple Arrivals=== Some content such as [[Treasure trials]], [[Barrows]], and [[Zulrah]] drops items in groups. ::*Let S \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\} ::*Let q(S) be the probability to receive a drop with none of the items in S.
E[T] = \sum_{S \neq \emptyset}(-1)^{\left|S\right|+1}\frac{1}{1 - q(S)}{{CiteGeneral|url=https://arxiv.org/pdf/1209.2667|title=A note on the coupon - collector’s problem with multiple arrivals and the random sampling|author=Marco Ferrante and Nadia Frigo|work=arXiv|year=2024|pages=5-9}}
When developing the specific formula for q(S) content such as Zulrah has groups that are drawn independently with replacement. Treasure trails has groups which are also drawn with replacement, but are variable in size. Barrows is drawn without replacement within each group.{{efn|See the [[Talk:Chest_(Barrows)]] page for many Expected Waiting Time and Probability formulas.}} For the basic independent replacement draws: ::*Let g be the number of rolls for items available in each group.
q(S) = \left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^g
For Treasure trails: ::*Let g be the median number of rolls for items from each clue.
q(S) = \frac{1}{3} \left(\left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g-1} + \left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g} + \left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g+1}\right)
This formula has the same computational issue of the singular draw [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusion%E2%80%93exclusion_principle Inclusion-Exclusion] formula. Because the formula needs to pass over all combinations of subsets it requires 2^{n}-1 terms. However, the formula can be simplified when items share drop rates. By calculating q(S) for each unique subset only and then multiplying each term of the summation by the number of subsets that share the same q(S). ::*Items are partitioned into R classes: ::*class r has probability p_r. ::*class r has q_r items.{{efn|The Q quantities in this context are the number of unique items that share the same drop rate. This is distinctly different than the K quotas in the previous section where the same item is desired multiple items.}} ::*Let a_r be how many items from class r are in subset S.
\left|S\right| = \sum_{r=1}^{R}a_r q(S) = \left(1 - \sum_{r=1}^{R}a_r p_r\right)^{g} E\left[T\right] = \sum_{S \neq \emptyset}(-1)^{\left|S\right|+1}\left(\prod_{r=1}^R \binom{q_r}{a_r}\right)\frac{1}{1 - q(S)}
Example: A player wants to complete the [[Medium treasure trails]] Collection log.
P = \left\{\frac{1}{2266},\frac{1}{1133},\frac{1}{314}\right\} Q = \left\{18,94,3\right\} g = 4 q(S) = \frac{1}{3} \left(\left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g-1} + \left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g} + \left(1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\right)^{g+1}\right) E\left[_4T_Q(P)\right] \approx 2076.595979{{efn|The precise value is a fraction with a 13,593 digit numerator and 13,590 digit denominator. Float conversion presented for space concerns. Python's Sympy computer algebra package used for calculation.}}
The Multiple Arrivals formula generally requires computer assistance to compute due to the large number of terms. However, if only an approximate result is desired the singular draw integral solution can be used with np as the adjusted probabilities. The probabilities p for receiving each specific item from all tiers of clue scrolls are p \approx (10^{-2},10^{-5}). These probabilities are sufficiently small such that \left(\left(1-p\right)^{n-1}+\left(1-p\right)^{n}+\left(1-p\right)^{n+1}\right)\frac{1}{3} \approx \left(1-p\right)^{n} and therefore one can simply use the average number of reward rolls instead of the full distribution of reward rolls. Also \left(1-p\right)^n \approx e^{-np} and therefore one can use the standard singular draw integral solution to the coupon collector's problem. Using e^{-np} the [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=Integrate%5B1-%281-e%5E%28-4t%2F2266%29%29%5E18%281-e%5E%28-4t%2F1133%29%29%5E94%281-e%5E%28-4t%2F341%29%29%5E3%2C%7Bt%2C0%2C%E2%88%9E%7D%5D approximate result] is < 1 clue different than the true result. ===General Solution (Markov Chains)=== The formulas presented thus far offer closed form expression to solve the Coupon Collect's Problem with various complications. However, they all must be applied carefully to item sets which have drop mechanics that fall in to their domain. [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absorbing_Markov_chain Absorbing Markov Chains] offer a general solution to any coupon collector question. The trade offs are that Markov Chain process is an algorithm rather than a closed form expression, the complexity is offloaded to the transition probability formula, and sets with large numbers of states become computationally intractable. One distinct advantage Markov Chains have over the formula present above is handling [[tertiary drops]]. All of the formulas above assume that all of the items desired come from the same overall [[drop table]]; however, many items like pets and jars are dropped in addition to the boss' standard drop table. Example: [[crazy archaeologist]] has one tertiary drop in addition to two standard drops on its collection log. The expected waiting time to complete the collection log is:
Drop Rates = \left\{\frac{1}{256},\frac{1}{256},\frac{1}{128}\right\}
::There are 2^3 possible log states. Define p_{ij} as the probability of transitioning from state i to state j. Construct a 2^3 by 2^3 matrix,P, representing all possible states and populate the matrix with the transition probabilities.
P = \begin{bmatrix} 16129/16384 & 127/16384 & 127/32768 & 1/32768 & 127/32768 & 1/32768 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 127/128 & 0 & 1/256 & 0 & 1/256 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 32385/32768 & 255/32768 & 0 & 0 & 127/32768 & 1/32768\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 255/256 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/256\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 32385/32768 & 255/32768 & 127/32768 & 1/32768\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 255/256 & 0 & 1/256\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 127/128 & 1/128\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
::Extract the transient states in to a sub-matrix, Q. ::Let N := \sum_{k=0}^\infty Q^k = (I - Q)^{-1} where ''I'' is the identity matrix of size Q. ::The expected number of steps before being absorbed in any absorbing state, when starting in transient state ''i'' can be computed via a sum over transient states. The value is given by the ''i''th entry of the vector T := N \mathbf{1}, where '''1''' is a column vector whose entries are all 1.
T = \begin{bmatrix} 39567872/97665\\ 384\\ 114304/383\\ 256\\ 114304/383\\ 256\\ 128 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \text{Missing all items state}\\ \text{Missing both shards state}\\ \text{Missing Odium shard and Fedora state}\\ \text{Missing Odium shard state}\\ \text{Missing Malediction shard and Fedora state}\\ \text{Missing Malediction shard state}\\ \text{Missing fedora state} \end{bmatrix}
::The expect waiting time to complete the Crazy archeologist log of 39567872/97665 \approx 405.139 is very closely approximated by the singular draw formula. ::E[T_n(P)] = \int_0^{\infty}\left(1-\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{256}}\right)^{2}\left(1-e^{-\frac{t}{128}}\right)\right)dt = \frac{1216}{3} \approx [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=Integrate%5B1+-+%281+-+Exp%5B-t%2F4095%5D%29*%281+-+Exp%5B-t%2F1365%5D%29%5E2*%281+-+Exp%5B-8+t%2F512%5D%29*%281+-+Exp%5B-3+t%2F512%5D%29%2C+%7Bt%2C0%2CInfinity%7D%5D 405.333] ::The proper treatment of the tertiary nature of the [[fedora]] has little impact on the overall waiting time since the likelihood of receiving it along with a Shard is \ll1. This is true generally. Most drops in the game are sufficiently rare such that treating tertiary drops as if they were dropped from the standard drop table has little impact on the expected waiting time. Markov Chain solutions can also handle multiple absorption states. For example, what is the expected waiting time to complete a full set of [[oathplate armour]] accounting for [[oathplate shards]] crafting?{{efn|573.375 solo kills. Calculated with floats in Python's Numpy computer algebra package.}} This could be achieved by constructing a transition matrix with states \left(0,0\right) to \left(3,1350\right) where the first index is how many unique oathplate pieces the player has and the second is how many shards.
